say: Good morning Steven. Here's your Avalanche Briefing for Thursday, November nineteenth.

scenes.headline: No danger ratings yet
scenes.source: NWAC Snow and Avalanche Discussion · Schiff and Lazzara · Wed Nov 18, 6 PM
say: The Northwest Avalanche Center hasn't started daily danger ratings yet, so all ten zones show no rating today.
Until daily forecasts begin, forecasters post an early season Snow and Avalanche Discussion every Monday, Wednesday and Friday evening.
The latest came out Wednesday evening from Payton Schiff and Lee Lazzara, and it covers every zone.
Let's start with Snoqualmie Pass, your home zone.

scenes.headline: Thin snow, rocks still showing
scenes.note: Enough snow up high for avalanches; obstacles are the bigger risk
scenes.source: NWAC Snow and Avalanche Discussion · Schiff and Lazzara · Wed Nov 18, 6 PM
say: There's no danger rating at Snoqualmie Pass today or tomorrow.
October storms brought the first snow, but warm atmospheric rivers in early November melted much of it away.
Snow cover is limited, but upper elevations hold enough snow to ride, and enough for avalanches.
The forecasters say exposed or partly buried rocks and stumps are likely the biggest hazard right now.

scenes.headline: Three things to watch
scenes.source: NWAC Snow and Avalanche Discussion · Schiff and Lazzara · Wed Nov 18, 6 PM
rows: A small slide can push you into them
Shallow, patchy snow; budget extra time
say: First, small avalanches.
Look for pockets of wind drifted snow along and just below the downwind side of ridgelines.
If the sun comes out, watch for rollerballs and snow shedding off rocks and trees, which are early signs of wet snow instability.
Second, terrain traps.
With so little snow, even a small slide could push you into rocks or over cliffs, so pay attention to what's below you.
Third, slow travel.
Shallow, patchy snow hides rocks and stumps, so keep your plan simple, steer around steep slopes, and budget extra time.

scenes.headline: Dry Friday, damp weekend
scenes.source: NWAC Mountain Weather · Dallas Glass · Wed Nov 18, 1:46 PM
rows: Then mostly dry, 25 to 31°F at 5,000 ft
Light east winds at the ridges
say: Now the mountain weather for Snoqualmie Pass, from Wednesday afternoon's forecast.
Expect only a trace to one inch of new snow through Friday, then mostly dry weather, with temperatures from twenty five to thirty one degrees at five thousand feet.
Freezing levels run from three thousand to forty five hundred feet Thursday and Friday, with light east winds along the ridges.
This weekend, a low pressure trough off the coast sends bands of precipitation our way, with snow levels around two thousand to twenty five hundred feet.
Forecasters say the weekend looks damp at the very least, and how much snow falls depends on where that trough sets up.

scenes.headline: Light snow; most near Mission Ridge
scenes.source: NWAC Mountain Weather and Snow and Avalanche Discussion · Wed Nov 18
say: Here's a quick look at the other zones.
On the west slopes, Crystal and Paradise were forecast to get one to three inches from Wednesday night's storm, Stevens Pass and Hurricane Ridge only a trace to an inch, and none at Mount Baker.
East of the crest, east winds favored the Wenatchee Mountains, with four to six inches forecast near Mission Ridge and one to three inches in the Tieton area.
On Mount Hood, forecasters found only a thin layer of snow at five thousand feet, but considerably more by sixty five hundred feet.
Across the region, the most consistent snow is in high alpine terrain, especially on the volcanoes.

rows: No danger rating yet; thin, patchy snow
say: Bottom line for Snoqualmie: no danger rating yet, with thin and patchy snow.
The biggest hazard is hitting rocks, stumps and terrain traps, not big avalanches.
Watch for fresh drifts below ridgelines, and rollerballs if the sun comes out.
The next update from the Northwest Avalanche Center is Friday at six in the evening.
Always read the full forecast before you head out, and share what you see with the Northwest Avalanche Center.
That's your Avalanche Briefing. Stay safe out there.
